Luggage refers to the bags, suitcases, and other containers that a person uses to carry their personal belongings while traveling. When you are going on a trip — whether by plane, train, ship, or bus — everything you pack your clothes and items into is your luggage.

Think of it this way: the moment you start filling a bag to go somewhere, that bag (and everything like it you are bringing) becomes your luggage.

Luggage is a broad word. It covers many types of travel containers, including suitcases, travel bags, duffel bags, backpacks (when used for a trip), and trunks. Basically, if you are traveling and you are carrying it, it is luggage.
A critical grammar point — luggage is uncountable

This is one of the most important things to know about this word. Luggage is an uncountable noun. This means:

  • ❌ You cannot say "a luggage"
  • ❌ You cannot say "two luggages"
  • ✅ You say "luggage" or "some luggage"
  • ✅ If you want to count it, you say "a piece of luggage" or "two pieces of luggage"

Because it is uncountable, it always takes a singular verb:

  • ✅ "My luggage is heavy." (not "are heavy")
  • ✅ "The luggage was lost."
Where and how you will see it used

Luggage appears most often in travel-related situations. Here are the most natural and common ways to use it:

At an airport:

  • "Please place your luggage on the scale."
  • "My luggage was lost by the airline."
  • "You can collect your luggage at the baggage carousel." (the moving belt where bags arrive after a flight)

At a hotel:

  • "The porter carried our luggage to the room."
  • "Can you store my luggage at the front desk until my room is ready?"

General travel:

  • "I travel light — I only take one piece of luggage."
  • "Don't leave your luggage unattended."
The most common expressions with luggage

These are fixed phrases that native speakers use all the time. Knowing them will make you sound natural.

Checked luggage — luggage that you hand over to the airline at the counter before a flight. It goes into the bottom of the plane (the hold) and you collect it when you land.

Carry-on luggage / hand luggage — the smaller bag you are allowed to bring inside the plane cabin with you and put in the overhead compartment. ("Carry-on" is more American; "hand luggage" is more British.)

Excess luggage — luggage that is heavier or bigger than what the airline allows. You usually have to pay extra for it.

Luggage allowance — the amount of luggage (by weight or number of bags) that you are permitted to bring on a flight for free.

Luggage rack — a shelf or storage space above seats (on a train or plane) where you can put your bags.

Luggage tag / luggage label — a small card attached to a bag that shows the owner's name, address, or destination, so it can be identified if lost.

Lost luggage — luggage that an airline has misplaced and cannot immediately locate.
Luggage vs. Baggage — what is the difference?

These two words mean almost exactly the same thing. Both are uncountable. However, there are small differences in how they are used:

  • Luggage is the more everyday, conversational word, especially in British English. When you talk about packing and carrying your bags, "luggage" sounds more natural.
  • Baggage is slightly more formal and is commonly used in official and airline contexts ("baggage claim," "baggage drop"). It is also more dominant in American English.

In most real-life situations, the two words can be used interchangeably and anyone will understand you perfectly either way.

One important note: "baggage" (but generally not "luggage") can be used figuratively to describe emotional burdens a person carries from past experiences — for example, "She has a lot of emotional baggage from her difficult childhood." Luggage does not carry this figurative meaning, so stick to using it only in the literal, travel-related sense.
